content: Pregnant women were less likely to report receiving an influenza vaccination in the past 12 months (9.6%) compared to non-pregnant women (15.7%). Vaccination coverage among pregnant women remained relatively unchanged between 1997 and 1999, whereas coverage among non-pregnant women increased from 14.4% in 1997. Similar findings were observed using data from the 1997–2000 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), excluding pregnant women with diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, or other high-risk conditions (unpublished NHIS data, NIP, CDC, 2002). In a study on influenza vaccine acceptance among pregnant women, 71% of those offered the vaccine chose to be vaccinated. However, a 1999 survey of obstetricians and gynecologists found that only 39% administered the influenza vaccine to obstetric patients, despite 86% agreeing that pregnant women face increased risks of influenza-related morbidity and mortality during the last two trimesters. The influenza vaccine is strongly recommended for individuals aged >6 months who are at increased risk for complications from influenza. Additionally, healthcare workers and others in close contact with high-risk individuals should be vaccinated to reduce the risk of transmitting influenza to these vulnerable populations. The vaccine can also be administered to any individual aged >6 months to reduce the likelihood of influenza infection. Vaccination is particularly recommended for individuals aged 50–64 years, as this group has a higher prevalence of high-risk medical conditions. Approximately 43 million people in the United States fall into this age group, with 10–14 million (24%–32%) having at least one high-risk condition (unpublished data, NIP, CDC, 2002). Influenza vaccination has been recommended for this entire age group to address low vaccination rates among those with high-risk conditions. Age-based strategies have proven more effective in increasing vaccine coverage than strategies targeting individuals based on medical conditions. Even those aged 50–64 years without high-risk conditions benefit from vaccination through reduced influenza illness rates, decreased work absenteeism, and fewer medical visits and medication needs, including antibiotics. Furthermore, age 50 is a critical time for initiating other preventive services, including routine vaccination assessments. Individuals who are clinically or subclinically infected can transmit the influenza virus to high-risk individuals. Reducing transmission from caregivers to high-risk individuals may decrease influenza-related deaths in this population. Evidence from two studies indicates that vaccinating healthcare workers is associated with reduced mortality among nursing home patients. Vaccination of healthcare workers and others in close contact with high-risk individuals, including household members, is recommended. Specific groups that should be vaccinated include physicians, nurses, emergency medical personnel, employees of nursing homes and chronic-care facilities, and household members of high-risk individuals. Because children aged 0–23 months are at increased risk for influenza-related hospitalization, vaccination is encouraged for their household contacts and out-of-home caregivers, particularly for contacts of children aged 0–5 months, as influenza vaccines are not approved for use in children under 6 months of age by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Influenza-associated excess deaths among pregnant women were documented during the pandemics of 1918–1919 and 1957–1958. Case reports and limited studies suggest that pregnancy increases the risk of severe influenza complications due to physiological changes such as increased heart rate, stroke volume, oxygen consumption, decreased lung capacity, and altered immunologic function. A study of 17 interpandemic influenza seasons demonstrated that the relative risk of hospitalization for selected cardiorespiratory conditions among pregnant women enrolled in Medicaid increased from 1.4 during weeks 14–20 of gestation to 4.7 during weeks 37–42, compared to women who were 1–6 months postpartum. Women in their third trimester were hospitalized at a rate comparable to non-pregnant women with high-risk medical conditions. Based on this study, researchers estimated that 1–2 hospitalizations could be prevented for every 1,000 pregnant women vaccinated. Due to the increased risk of influenza-related complications, women beyond the first trimester of pregnancy (>14 weeks of gestation) during influenza season should be vaccinated. Pregnant women with medical conditions that increase their risk for influenza complications should be vaccinated before the influenza season, regardless of pregnancy stage. A study of influenza vaccination in over 2,000 pregnant women found no adverse fetal effects associated with the vaccine. However, additional data are needed to confirm the safety of vaccination during pregnancy. Most influenza vaccines distributed in the United States contain thimerosal, a mercury-containing compound, as a preservative, though vaccines with reduced thimerosal content may be available in limited quantities.
